25fd86bf5115.text: Institutional agricultural channels are more plausible near-term partners than assuming every individual grower is the buyer. Field handling practices and pain points exist, but a broad multi-crop story still read as “technology looking for a use.”

db78d37193db.text: The sensing element — not electronics alone — is where industry remains stuck

a92beea6955f.text: Showing that AeroSense can detect odor — with strong electronics and algorithms — would be enough to compete. We needed to know what a VOC sensor must do for people who already ship electronic noses — not what makes a demo look good.

545ddd256610.text: Priorities: selectivity, field-robust sensitivity, lifetime, and reproducibility. The sensing element — not electronics alone — is where industry remains stuck.

8dc3c40ed238.text: Reframed AeroSense differentiation around the biological sensing layer and the hardware noise-rejection path needed to protect faint signals. Keep the biological receptor layer as the differentiation bet; require hardware noise-rejection (for example lock-in readout) so faint signals survive real environments.

8f4b9f8ce631.text: Technical-loop interview on sensing-element priorities under real deployment conditions. Company naming pending. Revalidation: staged hardware validation and field-like noise tests — not demo-only traces — remains pending. No original dated note or photo-permission record is archived.

283eba9e71e2.text: Mold VOC detection can be described directly as food-safety detection. Choose an attractive application first (for example mold detection), then find receptor targets that fit it.

8ab5eb96d8e3.text: Start from the technology, not the application — establish what AeroSense can actually distinguish before locking a market claim. Mold VOCs do not necessarily represent food safety — processing can kill viable fungi or change their odor profile while a toxin such as aflatoxin remains, so a mold-VOC signal and an actual safety verdict are not the same claim.

a824f8439730.text: Use “VOC risk screening”; avoid definitive safe/unsafe claims; route high-risk samples to confirmatory laboratory testing; report risk tier with visible confidence. Adopted the target-selection framework: Detectability × Consequence × Unmet Need × Willingness to Pay. Separated the agricultural beachhead from a longer-horizon food-safety / pathogen-VOC thread on the same platform.

2fe8b179942e.text: Completed industry interview (team record; paraphrases on IHP). Individual speaker names are not published here. Formal regulatory / biotech-law advice remains planned. Filling framework cells with measured detectability and buyer evidence remains pending — not literature hypotheses alone.

46633bb0fe75.text: On-site screening before confirmation — not a cheaper GC-MS

5d3d61db1055.text: AeroSense could be positioned as a cheaper, faster alternative that stands in for conventional laboratory analytical instruments. The individual agricultural grower is the obvious first customer for a field VOC tool.

2f1716e4cb8f.text: Amortized instrument cost is not the prohibitive barrier assumed; trained personnel and infrastructure are. Individual growers often resist tools that flag their own product. Industry is already moving toward smaller mobile labs. Laboratory assays are already strong at identification; in many workflows their limits are time, destruction, infrastructure, and continuous impracticality — not the absence of analytical capability.

661d1753dc29.text: Position AeroSense as rapid, lower-burden, on-site screening before laboratory confirmation — Fast · On-site · Low operator dependence — an early decision-support layer, not a drop-in GC-MS substitute. Buyer segment corrected toward associations, stations, cooperatives, and certification bodies — without claiming any of them as a contracted customer.

075f70ae1611.text: Completed industry interview; documented in Engineering Cycle 3 and Entrepreneurship learning cards. Cost figures are interviewee-reported estimates. Exporter and packing-house interviews on workflow, loss ownership, and willingness to pay remain pending.

5bbcdd9bdd0e.text: AeroSense aims to turn smell into actionable data: a biologically inspired, AI-driven volatile organic compound (VOC) sensing platform combining a living olfactory receptor layer, custom lock-in optoelectronic hardware, and a neuromorphic classifier modeled on the fly brain. Human Practices guided its development toward a platform that people could buy, trust and use correctly, connecting the technology to its intended users and decisions.

6bce8683b2d5.text: Through completed interviews spanning agricultural field sites, industry electronic-nose specialists, food-safety biotechnology professionals, and mentor review panels, plus a public survey probing food-spoilage habits and trust in automated screening tools, we built a working understanding of where our sensing platform's real value lies — and, just as importantly, where it does not.

0dca51275a1e.text: Our mission — let machines smell at a biological level, and turn odor into a measurable data dimension — is only worth pursuing if it is built responsibly. Three values have anchored every design decision:

aa9f6d4c13b8.text: August 10, 2026 | Assistant Researcher Ya-Yun Chang, Plant Protection Laboratory, Taoyuan District Agricultural Research and Extension Station, Ministry of Agriculture

28553c8d013a.text: Every batch of produce and jar of dried food can begin to change before anyone sees it. Our screening concept targets VOC changes associated with fungal disease in banana shipments and spoilage in stored coffee or grain. The possibility of detecting these signals days to weeks before visible symptoms motivates the work; the lead time for each target remains a measurement to establish. Once a problem becomes visible, a batch may already have been shipped, mixed with healthy stock or consumed.

b8c9b1fe2ac9.text: Current options range from visual or manual inspection, which depends on visible symptoms, to laboratory assays such as PCR, ELISA and GC–MS, which require sampling, equipment and trained operation. Our team estimate of fungal-disease-related risk in the banana export beachhead is roughly NT$3.51 billion/year, calculated as 33.6% of an NT$10.445 billion annual sector-output baseline. This is a planning estimate, not a measured loss or a saving delivered by AeroSense. The same gap motivated our earlier stored-food theme: mold and mycotoxin screening for coffee, tea and dried goods.

0e0ffa66fae2.text: Our public survey reinforced the problem from the consumer side: most respondents understood that visible mold is a concern, but only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk. This pointed to a practical decision gap as well as an education need: people need information about a particular portion or batch. Low cost and a result within minutes became design goals, rather than measured performance claims.

c574e02411cb.text: Checking the problem in the field. We took this question to the Plant Protection Lab of the Taoyuan District Agricultural Improvement Station. A researcher there confirmed the gap from the grower's side: there is currently no monitoring method beyond looking at the crop, so no data are collected. The researcher then asked us the questions a farmer would: first confirm that the device can collect data, and for which disease; what the device would look like in a field, how many sampling points a plot would need, and what the returned data would mean; and that buying or licensing an instrument depends on the crop and the target. The researcher also mentioned an earlier proposal to drive a remote-controlled vehicle through a tea field to collect electronic-nose data — possible in theory, but still far from practical on uneven ground. We took this as a reminder that "detects a smell" and "works in a field" are different claims.

b9ad953df639.text: #2 Key considerations for the sensor: what would actually help industry (Chief Science Officer interview)

20f3807b8086.text: Before committing further engineering effort, we needed to know what a VOC sensor would have to do to be genuinely useful to people who already work with electronic-nose technology every day — not just what would make a compelling demo. We interviewed the Chief Science Officer (CSO) of an established domestic electronic-nose company Enosim Bio-Tech, whose own product line has already been evaluated against real deployment conditions.

84dbec51b381.text: The conversation reframed our engineering priorities around four properties, in this order of difficulty:

eb8919950670.text: Selectivity — a sensor that responds strongly and specifically to the target gas, not broadly to A, B, C, and D at once. The CSO was direct about the state of the market: almost no commercially available electronic nose today has genuinely high selectivity.

300b53caa193.text: Sensitivity — how low a concentration (down to ppm-level) the sensor can still detect, with a signal-to-noise ratio good enough to survive outside a quiet lab. This was flagged as the single most common failure mode: sensors that perform well on the bench become unusably noisy in a real field or warehouse environment.

a3776da0f77a.text: Reliability and lifetime — how long a sensor can be used before its response degrades. Replacing a sensor daily, as some current products effectively require, is not a workable answer for continuous monitoring (e.g., air-quality deployments).

93e558fda342.text: Reproducibility, including batch-to-batch consistency — does the same measurement, repeated, give the same answer; and do 100 units of the same sensor behave the same way as each other. This is a manufacturing-and-QA problem as much as a chemistry problem, and one the CSO said the industry still has not solved well.

0848d819a0b8.text: The CSO's central point was that the sensing element remains a major bottleneck: selectivity, sensitivity, stability and reproducibility matter before downstream electronics or signal processing can add value. This strengthened our decision to investigate biological receptors as a route to differentiation. The interview set a technical requirement; it did not validate AeroSense's selectivity or sensitivity.

232c37ed3f91.text: We treat this interview as belonging to the same evidence category as our technical-loop interviews: it does not tell us what to sell, but it does tell us the bar our sensing layer has to clear to be worth selling at all — and it directly shaped how we now describe our differentiation (see Box #4 and #6).

74c955c7339f.text: #3 Choice of the sensing platform, and why biology

4d3ac878da45.text: June 5, 2026 | Assistant Professor Huang, Post-Baccalaureate Program in Medicine, National Tsing Hua University

feca66b5f1b3.text: Given the CSO's framing — selectivity and sensitivity are where the market is actually stuck — we evaluated why AeroSense's approach (insect olfactory receptors expressed in a mammalian cell line, read out via calcium fluorescence) is structurally different from a metal-oxide, polymer, or piezoelectric electronic nose, rather than just a biological curiosity layered on top of the same old approach.

ae23899c3635.text: A conventional electronic nose uses a physical sensing material whose response is determined by its chemistry. AeroSense instead proposes an exchangeable biological sensing layer: cells express Drosophila OR/Orco receptors and a GCaMP6 calcium reporter, while changing the receptor gene can change the candidate target profile. Continued synthesis of receptor protein is a potential renewal mechanism. Whether it improves lifetime or drift compared with a static chemical film must be tested; living cells also introduce variability and maintenance requirements.

7314692d962d.text: The proposed cartridge uses genetically modified mammalian cells expressing the olfactory receptor and calcium reporter, so its handling and eventual use require institutional biosafety oversight and appropriate containment. Technology-transfer discussion is also relevant to the receptor and neuromorphic-layer research. The cartridge uses heterologous receptor expression rather than live insects. This distinction concerns the sensing cartridge; the separate light-sheet research uses Drosophila neural recordings.

e23c60de4856.text: #4 Receptor candidates and retrospective target analysis

10fd82fe770d.text: Receptor choice had to be evidence-driven. The early literature-candidate list in this Human Practices work contained seven receptors: Or10a, Or13a, Or47a, Or49b, Or71a, Or85b and Or98a. Zboray et al. (2023, Scientific Reports), a heterologous-expression ligand-profiling study directed at plant and plant-pathogen VOCs, informed this starting point. This early list is distinct from our final ten tuning-receptor modules documented in Parts and the Registry; it is not a record that all seven were cloned or tested.

2963f5222787.text: The Challenge Bio follow-up prompted a retrospective comparison between potential pathogen-indicator VOCs and the literature candidates. Or49b was considered for reported indole sensitivity, making it a candidate for future bacterial-VOC work rather than an already tested AeroSense receptor: Or49b is absent from the final ten-module experimental panel. Or13a and 1-octen-3-ol instead point back toward fungal volatiles; 1-octen-3-ol is widely known as mushroom alcohol and is not a bacteria-specific marker. These comparisons refined the target-selection question without establishing pathogen detection or specificity in our system.

7c83d66fff4f.text: A sensitive receptor is only as useful as the electronics that can read a faint fluorescence signal out of real-world noise. This is the CSO's point, that sensitivity in the lab often collapses in the field, and it is why we treated the readout circuit as a design problem of its own.

3b933f203a0b.text: Our first readout failed outside the lab. It used a blue LED and a camera. It worked on the bench, but once we left controlled conditions, ambient light and sensor noise swamped the faint cell signal. We replaced it with a lock-in design: the excitation light is modulated at a known frequency, and digital lock-in amplification (DLIA) reads only the signal at that frequency, rejecting room light and slow drift. We are candid about its limits. Excitation light that leaks onto the detector at the same frequency survives lock-in, so emission filtering, blank wells and per-well calibration are still needed.

a08a15bd5a16.text: Then we asked people with more hardware experience to check it. A circuit that only we had reviewed was the weakest link in the chain, so we took it to two sources of outside engineering advice.

a0fdf2bd71f5.text: Over several rounds, iST engineers reviewed our sensing circuit and board design and helped us get from schematic to a manufactured prototype. They checked how the photodiode was connected, the design of the first amplification stage, the signal-conversion wiring and filtering, and the power and grounding arrangement. They also helped us reposition the light source and detector so that the weak signal path stays short, and, across successive revisions, settle the parts list, sourcing and timeline. The most useful lesson came from testing the finished board. The first amplification stage had too much gain, so its output sat at saturation whatever the light level. The engineers advised us to try feedback components of different values until the gain matched the photocurrent we actually produce, rather than trusting our calculated figure. We could not yet confirm the fix: the test firmware and a matching test setup were not ready, so only the main power supply was measured before the board reached us.

9485bbdf642e.text: September 25, 2026 | A senior student with circuit-design experience

1dbbe08ce2f5.text: She came at the problem from the component side. She advised choosing the photodiode by its measured photocurrent, spectral response and current–voltage behavior, ideally with a device simulation, and confirming that the fluorescent protein's absorption and the light source's drive voltage actually match. For amplification she recommended a simple single-amplifier design with a suitable input range and a small feedback capacitor for stability and noise, and checking that the signal fits the converter's input range. She also stressed clean power, with proper smoothing at the regulator, and layout habits that cut noise: sensible trace routing, keeping the amplifier beside the detector, and large ground areas.

546df33f37fc.text: What changed. Three things. We now select the detector by its measured behavior instead of by what was convenient. Gain tuning, a signal measurement against known light levels, and then system integration are our next steps, in that order. And noise reduction, power stability and grounding moved from "later" to explicit goals of the next board revision. Where the hardware stands today: a first prototype board has been fabricated, but only its main power supply has been verified; light detection and signal conversion are untested until the firmware is ready.

da9399d99dd8.text: Computation. Our neuromorphic classification work follows the fly mushroom body's PN–KC–MBON odor-coding circuit and the research lineage of our advisors' Science Advances 2025 paper. It is intended to classify multichannel signals. The modeling results and the living-cell/hardware measurements remain separate evidence streams until end-to-end integration is demonstrated.

628f407bc72d.text: A result that arrives after the batch has already spoiled or shipped is not useful, however accurate it is. We optimize for detecting change before it is visible — the entire premise of a VOC platform.

7e632610aff3.text: Industry engineers and public survey respondents prompted us to make uncertainty visible. We designed the proposed output around a risk tier and a confidence signal, rather than a black-box binary verdict or a promise of certainty.

0769ee29f013.text: Modularity over a single fixed claim

e3fe884666d5.text: AeroSense is designed as a programmable receptor library rather than a device fixed to one target. That flexibility requires target-by-target evidence before making an application claim; our first application, mold detection, still needs its own validation.

7b43dd4d5e7b.text: #6 Refining the beachhead and the target-selection framework

bbd0e77eaf1e.text: Our application focus changed through mentor review, technical critique, instrumentation advice and field pathology. Each round changed the question we needed to test next.

c3b3e17bb129.text: Round one (mentor review, BP and pitch-deck feedback).

6cd7161a1683.text: August 15, 2026 | Industry Mentors (Investors), From IP to IPO (FITI) Program

3ff9c67ead6c.text: Our original framing covered six candidate crops (dragon fruit, passion fruit, strawberry, grape, citrus, banana) under a broad "facility agriculture pest detection" umbrella. Mentor review was blunt about the effect this had: "Right now it reads more like 'we have an electronic-nose technology that can do a lot of things,' but FITI needs to see 'a specific group of customers with a clear, expensive problem — and our odor detection directly reduces their loss, raises their price, or sets a new standard.'" This drove us to narrow to a single, economically quantifiable beachhead — banana disease detection in Taiwan's export supply chain — with mango and tea as explicit follow-on markets, and to reframe the whole narrative as a B2B Agricultural VOC Intelligence Platform rather than a general-purpose electronic nose.

669df731d16f.text: Just as we had converged on a single beachhead, a separate conversation with biotechnology industry professionals challenged the premise underneath our original food-safety framing, not the agricultural one: "Start from the technology, not the application" — establish what AeroSense can actually distinguish (detectable VOCs, specificity, sensitivity, response time, interference tolerance) before assuming any one market is the right one. Just as importantly: "mold VOCs do not necessarily represent food safety" — food processing can kill viable fungi or change their odor profile while a toxin such as aflatoxin remains, so a mold-VOC signal and an actual safety verdict are not the same claim, and we should not let our own marketing imply otherwise.

3f5b5b262f29.text: This produced an explicit target-selection framework: Detectability × Consequence × Unmet Need × Willingness to Pay. We use it to compare candidate applications rather than defaulting to mold detection, including the literature-based indole/Or49b candidate discussed in #4.

f3db44b1c22b.text: September 17, 2026 | SCIEX Field Service Engineer Lin (LC and GC–MS Maintenance)

668e8ccf7c48.text: We interviewed a professional with hands-on GC-MS/LC-MS testing-service experience Engineer to answer a question the first two rounds had left open: should AeroSense compete with laboratory instruments on analytical accuracy, or solve a different problem entirely? Their answer showed that our original assumption — that AeroSense would be "a cheaper alternative to conventional analytical instruments" — did not hold on the numbers: a GC-MS/LC-MS system's amortized cost (roughly NT$5–10 million over a ~15-year service life, plus NT$200,000–300,000/year maintenance, per the interviewee) is not the barrier we assumed; the real barriers are trained personnel and lab infrastructure, which is why the industry itself is already moving toward smaller and mobile testing units. We therefore repositioned our value proposition around three words the interviewee's account of the market supported: Fast · On-site · Low operator dependence — a rapid on-site screening layer that flags suspicious samples for laboratory confirmation, not a replacement for the lab.

349765d62925.text: Two further findings reshaped our thinking. First, individual farmers may have low willingness to pay and may resist having their own product flagged as a problem, which shifts our realistic B2B buyer toward farmers' associations, agricultural agencies, cooperatives, and certification bodies. Second, the interview surfaced a candidate application we had not evaluated — authenticity and origin verification (e.g., honey origin, tea authenticity) — as a third candidate alongside disease/ripeness detection and pathogen-VOC food-safety screening, though with its own validation challenge, since false positives and blended samples are harder to resolve than a straightforward risk flag. The interviewee also named two segments we had not considered, the semiconductor industry and humanitarian/logistics shipping; we record them as leads from a single conversation, not validated opportunities. All figures here are the interviewee's own and we have not independently verified them.

1ddbac0d9646.text: September 25, 2026 | Min-Hsiung Weng, Retired Researcher, Taiwan Banana Research Institute

10d432a0835c.text: To test where odor-based screening would help most on a banana farm, we interviewed a pest-and-disease specialist at the Taiwan Banana Research Institute in Pingtung and went through his institute's growth-stage guide to banana pests and diseases. Two findings stood out. First, the strongest odors come from below ground and basal tissue, not from the fruit: corm and pseudostem weevils, bacterial soft rot, crown rot, and Fusarium wilt (Panama disease), which smells strongest in the corm's vascular tissue. Fruit-side problems such as scale insects, finger-tip rot, and cigar-end rot are not strongly scented, and sooty mold smells faint. Second, the odor of Fusarium wilt is most obvious late, when the plant is already rotting and visibly blackened; he told us a faint signal is present earlier, though usually only noticeable in the middle to late stage, and that detecting it is largely a matter of sensor sensitivity. He also cautioned that a heavy pseudostem smell often just reflects a dirty orchard, so any odor reading has to be interpreted against field hygiene, and he named rot detection as a problem farmers and field workers need solved.

79f7e2972ad3.text: The interview also touched on who would use a tool like ours. He indicated that an institute like his is more willing to pay than individual farmers, which matches what the instrumentation interview told us. His institute already covers rot testing and pest-and-disease control close to growers, so it could be an entry point that reaches farmers who cannot buy a tool themselves; we are considering its Pingtung site as a pilot. He also asked the question we cannot yet answer: can the method really measure accurately, and are there particular diseases or sites where it works best? This is an expert's qualitative judgment, not a measurement, so we treat it as a hypothesis to test — how many days earlier the faint signal appears, and whether it can be separated from background orchard odor. It also pushes us to weigh field-level rot detection alongside our original post-harvest focus.

4bfae611c681.text: July–September 2026 | FITI (From IP to IPO) Program

a02ad5523d4e.text: We engaged directly with startup-support programs and mentor panels to pressure-test our commercialization plan rather than developing it in isolation. Selection into FITI (From IP to IPO), Taiwan's national innovation and entrepreneurship incentive program, and the 18th cohort of NTHU Garage connected us to structured, written mentor review at two stages: an 11-point review of our full business plan, and a separate slide-level review of our pitch deck. Both reviews converged on the same underlying instruction — lead with a specific customer's expensive problem, not with the technology — but each forced a different layer of revision: the BP review drove the beachhead narrowing and a full TAM/SAM/SOM rebuild (from a benchmark against the global electronic-nose instrument market to a bottom-up agricultural-VOC estimate connected to actual banana-sector loss figures); the pitch-deck review drove the competitive-analysis redesign (comparing detectable-VOC range, detection limit, and fingerprinting ability rather than analysis cycle time, an axis where we are not competitive) and a shift from a name-and-photo team slide to a capability matrix. The full stage-by-stage record is in our FITI Iteration Report.

c30704b194c8.text: Our financial model reflects this same discipline: modeled, not promised, figures — a Year 1 operating expense of roughly NT$3.08 million against a NT$3 million seed round in progress, with device and cartridge pricing (device ~NT$120,000, cartridge subscription ~NT$4,000/month) drawn from the same workbook rather than invented for a slide.

b93ad129823f.text: #7.2 Protecting what we built: a patent attorney consultation

4f3539d6b440.text: We consulted Patent Attorney Hsu, whose expertise includes pharmaceuticals and microbiology. She asked for the related paper, the device-design process and the reasoning behind each choice, together with a clear statement of the innovative technical step. Her advice led us to organize those materials and plan a prior-art search before selecting further experiments to strengthen the case.

ca41d75369e6.text: The consultation compared possible protection for engineered proteins with protection for the assembled device or system, and considered patents versus trade secrets. These remained strategic options to assess with the university and qualified counsel; the conversation did not establish a filing, granted right or infringement conclusion.

50c65c176ad8.text: The main design-management lesson concerned disclosure timing. We were advised to coordinate publication with a filing strategy, identify target jurisdictions and begin through the university technology-transfer route. We therefore added prior-art review, clarification of applicants and inventors, and a disclosure plan to our next actions. Jurisdiction-specific exceptions and filing consequences require separate professional assessment.

f976aba47224.text: Positive impacts. Earlier, non-destructive screening could help reduce food loss and unnecessary disposal if it provides useful information at the point of decision. The public survey found that only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk, showing why appearance alone is an inadequate decision rule. Our aim is to support triage of suspicious batches for confirmation, not to certify a batch as safe. Associations and cooperatives are intended routes for extending access to smaller producers; affordability and the resulting benefit still need to be measured.

ca9ef1a9f5f1.text: Risks to manage. An automated risk score that is trusted too much invites exactly the failure mode our own stakeholders warned us about from two directions at once: our public survey found that respondents ranked avoiding a missed real risk (a false negative) among their top needs from a screening tool, and the Challenge Bio interview independently warned that a mold-VOC signal is not the same claim as a food-safety verdict. Both point to the same design discipline: report a risk tier with an honest confidence signal and a recommendation to send high-risk samples for confirmatory lab testing — never a silent, false "safe" — and say plainly, in our own materials, what the tool does not certify. We plan a lightweight, mentor-supported data-governance check-in as the platform moves from single-partner pilots to multi-partner deployment, extending the same "close the loop, don't just collect feedback" discipline documented throughout this page to how we handle an increasingly large, cross-partner VOC dataset.

f9e280b36e84.text: #9 Handing the work on: from a science camp to a teacher toolkit

96e0801331c0.text: Most of this page asks what outsiders told us about our project. The last loop we closed ran the other way: we took our project to a school, and the school told us what it needed from us.

b3d16e40eefb.text: What we assumed. After the survey and games, we ran a half-day science camp at Shan-chi Elementary School in Xinfeng Township, Hsinchu County, on October 12, 2026, for more than thirty fifth-grade pupils. We initially treated the visit as the finished product: children explored the relation between a nose, an electronic nose and our sensor, played the game and drew their ideas. The full activity and learning records are on the Education page.

e12039be25d1.text: What we heard. We met the school's principal on the camp day. He told us he liked the way we teach, and he asked for a way to keep using it, since a team of university students cannot visit every year.

05833753a8d5.text: What it changed. His request moved the unit of impact from the visit to the lesson. If a school wants something it can keep using, a camp is the wrong thing to leave behind. We packaged the camp into a Teacher Toolkit: a 40-minute lesson with slides, a whole-class version of our game in which each team answers by holding up one, two or three fingers, a worksheet, and instructions for using our online Learning Lab, so that a teacher who has never met us can run the same session. The school welcomed the approach, and the toolkit is free for any teacher to download. The same conversation gave us the design rule that opens our Education Guide for other teams: write the plan so that someone who has never met you can run it.

e0bea0e8e428.text: Read the screening and buyer analysis

41a601bcd27c.text: Open the Teacher Toolkit and Education Guide

d210198ccb03.text: Earlier decision summaries and implementation details

74999b8c6861.text: Professor Cheng, Enosim Bio-Tech CSO; 11 September 2026

1d614840a367.text: SCIEX Field Service Engineer Lin; 17 September 2026

e600887d2323.text: We sought out events where people working in synthetic biology, biotechnology, agriculture and commercialization could test our assumptions. Some discussions changed a number in the business plan; others changed how we described the project.

c40ec16a69a9.text: Our entry point into structured commercialization support was selection into the 18th cohort of NTHU Garage, the university's entrepreneurship incubation program. This became our home base for the rest of the season: regular access to mentor office hours, a structured go-to-market and fundraising curriculum. NTHU Garage is where our very first business-plan draft took shape, before any of the external review rounds that reshaped it.

d49aeb662168.text: We reached out to the S.Y.Dao Cancer Prevention Foundation after learning that olfactory-based sensing had shown promise for early cancer detection — close enough to our own platform that we approached them on our own initiative rather than waiting for a polished pitch. Through the discussion, we brought our Food & Nutrition-track VOC findings together with our platform's potential medical application, rather than presenting the two as separate stories. The foundation responded positively to both the technology and its application potential.

7afbd52cf266.text: We presented AeroSense's platform at SynBioBeta 2026, an international synthetic-biology industry conference, via a poster session aimed at an industry rather than academic audience. b19d67c67ce1.text: AeroSense combines living olfactory receptors, lock-in optoelectronic hardware and a fly-inspired classifier to investigate VOC screening. Human Practices connected these technical choices to the people, workflows and decisions the platform is intended to serve.

07b6bd8045d8.text: Agricultural specialists, electronic-nose engineers, food-safety professionals, mentors and public survey respondents helped us define where screening could be useful and what evidence each application would require.

cbd88a972171.text: Three values guide how we turn odor into information people can act on:

77aab66a79e6.text: We asked the Chief Science Officer of Enosim Bio-Tech, a domestic electronic-nose company with deployment experience, what would make a VOC sensor useful in practice. The question set engineering priorities beyond a laboratory demonstration.

ab47a9175d9c.text: The CSO’s emphasis on selectivity and sensitivity sharpened our comparison of biological sensing with metal-oxide, polymer and piezoelectric electronic noses. AeroSense expresses insect olfactory receptors in mammalian cells and reads their response through calcium fluorescence.

4d8bb5ddc2d2.text: This technical interview set the sensing requirements behind our differentiation and target selection in #4 and #6.

2d0c330850f6.text: The CSO’s warning about performance outside the lab made fluorescence readout a separate design problem: the electronics must recover a faint signal under environmental noise.

4b4adaf1b4dd.text: Our first readout used a blue LED and camera. It worked on the bench, but ambient light and sensor noise overwhelmed the faint cell signal outside controlled conditions. We moved to digital lock-in amplification (DLIA), modulating excitation at a known frequency and extracting that frequency to reject room light and slow drift. Same-frequency excitation leakage remains, so emission filtering, blank wells and per-well calibration are still required.

410877ed1408.text: We then sought two independent sources of engineering advice on the circuit and component choices.

f96589fe14fc.text: iST engineers reviewed successive schematics and board designs, helping us reach a manufactured prototype. They checked photodiode connections, first-stage amplification, signal-conversion wiring, filtering, power and grounding, shortened the light-source/detector signal path, and refined sourcing and the parts list. Testing exposed excessive first-stage gain: the output stayed saturated regardless of light level. They recommended varying feedback components to match the measured photocurrent. The fix remains unconfirmed because test firmware and a matching setup were not ready; only the main power supply was measured before delivery.

2ef59ae0f855.text: The senior student recommended selecting the photodiode by measured photocurrent, spectral response and current–voltage behavior, supported by device simulation. She also asked us to check fluorescent-protein absorption and light-source drive voltage; use a single amplifier with a suitable input range and small feedback capacitor; and keep the output within the converter’s range. Regulator smoothing, sensible routing, an amplifier beside the detector and large ground areas were priorities for stable power and lower noise.

a72924e33188.text: What changed. Detector selection now follows measured behavior. The test sequence is gain tuning, response to known light levels, then system integration; noise, power stability and grounding are explicit revision goals. The first board is fabricated, with its main supply verified. Light detection and conversion await test firmware.

e915e5906ddf.text: We asked whether AeroSense should compete with GC-MS/LC-MS instruments on analytical accuracy. The SCIEX engineer estimated a system at NT$5–10 million over a ~15-year life, plus NT$200,000–300,000/year maintenance. In his account, trained personnel and laboratory infrastructure were greater barriers than amortized instrument cost, motivating smaller and mobile testing units. We therefore shifted from a cheaper-instrument pitch to Fast · On-site · Low operator dependence: screening suspicious samples for laboratory confirmation.

d2bf3e6b22ec.text: He also questioned individual farmers’ willingness to pay and their willingness to have products flagged, shifting our buyer focus toward associations, agencies, cooperatives and certification bodies. Authenticity and origin verification—such as honey origin or tea authenticity—emerged alongside disease/ripeness detection and pathogen-VOC screening, with false positives and blended samples posing separate validation problems. Semiconductor and humanitarian/logistics applications were further leads from this one interview. The costs and market views remain the interviewee’s estimates, not independently verified findings.

8546e85d3cbb.text: FITI and the 18th cohort of NTHU Garage provided structured review of our commercialization plan: an 11-point business-plan review and a separate slide-level pitch review. Both asked us to lead with a customer’s expensive problem. The business-plan review narrowed the beachhead and rebuilt TAM/SAM/SOM from a global electronic-nose benchmark into a bottom-up agricultural-VOC estimate tied to banana-sector losses. The pitch review changed our comparison to detectable-VOC range, detection limit and fingerprinting ability, rather than analysis cycle time, and replaced a name-and-photo team slide with a capability matrix. The FITI Iteration Report records each revision.

b4be9db8970b.text: At the school, feedback changed what we chose to leave behind.

8b8039db0fc2.text: What it changed. We turned the visit into a Teacher Toolkit: a 40-minute lesson with slides, a class game answered by holding up one, two or three fingers, a worksheet and Learning Lab instructions. The school welcomed this way to repeat the session without our team, and teachers can download it free. This became the opening rule of our Education Guide: write the plan so someone who has never met you can run it.
